# Session Merge and Handoff System

We need a way to merge multiple originally separate sessions when they begin to overlap or converge on the same tasks or track. This should let us bring them back onto a shared track or shared ticket, and it is tightly coupled to handoff and orchestration.

## Current Direction

We may want, in the future, to coordinate essentially all work in this repository through a root session. In that model, a session would run all day, use subagents to handle found tasks, start reviews or subagents, complete individual tracks end to end, and interact with the user through interviews or messaging to gather new tasks and reviews. The goal would be to keep pushing progress across the repository.

That model is not realistic or practical yet. It carries a high risk of wasting tokens inefficiently, doing the wrong work, executing tasks incorrectly, or failing to verify acceptance criteria properly.

## Current Operating Model

For now, we are still in a model where sessions are started manually for specific tracks, specific tickets, or ad hoc per task. The main pattern we already use is structured handoff, which separates planning from implementation and isolates implementation from question-and-answer cycles.

We also already use orchestration where an agent runs multiple workflow steps and can delegate implementation or review to subagents. That is useful, but it is usually limited to an isolated goal and often does not run all the way through to the completion of a track. In practice, it usually completes only certain increments for a given track.

We also use the iteration agent to review and close implementations for a track or for specific tickets, and to clear the way for the next incremental implementation.

## Missing Capability

What is still missing is a way to merge sessions that started at different points but have developed toward the same tasks or the same track, and to redistribute work across multiple sessions that have substantial overlap.

For example, if three sessions in the session API project started with different tasks but then worked on overlapping tickets and dependencies, it can stop making sense to treat them as three separate sessions. Instead, the overlapping work should be merged into a single session that can explicitly reference the three original sessions, carry forward the work and past protocol, and implement the shared work with all context preserved.

We therefore need a complete handoff and pickup system, or a merge system, that allows sessions to be combined or split as needed. We also need clear provenance for every session, with references between sessions across handoffs and pickups or merge operations, so it is always documented which session handed off work to which other session, and which session picked up which other session.

These relationships must be many-to-many. A session must be able to initiate multiple other sessions through several handoffs, and a session must also be able to merge multiple other sessions into one through a pickup or merge step.

## Tracks and Graph Structure

Multiple sessions must also be assignable to a track. A track is a larger system of related tickets rooted in an epic or tracker ticket, and it should be possible to build a chain, tree, or full graph of sessions for that track.

Tracks can overlap, and they can also contain smaller tracks. The rule should be that sessions work on the smallest applicable track they belong to, and that the smaller track also knows which larger tracks use it.

This should allow an orchestrator to start multiple tracks, maintain a larger track that depends on smaller tracks, have the smaller tracks worked on by subagents in parallel or on different branches, and allow those smaller agents to create additional sessions for the same track or even start a smaller shared track used by both. The orchestrator can then merge the handoffs of the two tracks into a shared handoff or merge for the common track they both depend on, let another session work on that shared track, and then split back into handoffs for the original tracks once the shared work is complete.

The orchestrator should then be able to say that both of its tracks are finished, their shared dependency is complete, its own track can be closed, and the work can be handed off to the next session.

## Graph Materialization

Because these workflows are complex, the system must materialize all of these links as a full graph structure across the repository using references between entities and detailed session logging.

The task now is to fully work out this idea, materialize the complete plan, and close the gaps that still prevent us from understanding how to validate the system correctly, how to document the exact work steps for the agents, and how to break the whole plan into clear, goal-oriented steps.

## Planning Process

We should reuse as much of the already planned or already designed work as possible. We do not want to define something that is already planned or partially designed. Instead, we want to map the new idea onto the existing system and make sure every component has its place. We should only define new things when they do not yet exist in our planning.

The process should be:

1. First, understand the task better through an interview with the user about the details of the system, and derive a rough overall plan with a clearly defined shape, main goals, examples, and concrete acceptance criteria.
2. Then think through the individual components in detail and develop an initial structural design for the system.
3. Find those components in the existing plan so we can resolve conflicts or extensions of existing components.
4. Bring the previous plan into the new ticket track as dependencies so we can build directly on earlier requirements.
5. Update existing tickets if we discover extensions or conflicts, and regularly resolve important architectural questions with the user.
6. Create a large ticket track for the implementation plan, and use specifications to write down the goals, acceptance criteria, and chosen design.
7. The specification work can start with a single ticket whose purpose is to write the specs, but that should already be part of the overall plan.
8. Once the specs are fixed and the sequencing of work steps in the ticket track is complete, start implementation through orchestration and multiple subagents and sessions until all dependencies are implemented, satisfied, and fully validated.

# Session Merge and Pickup Workflow

We need a way to merge separately started sessions onto a shared track or ticket, and later split them apart again. This is important for handoff, orchestration, and keeping repository work coordinated.

## Current direction

- The long-term vision is a root session that coordinates most or all repository work for a day, starts subagents for tasks and reviews, and uses user interviews or messaging to collect new tasks.
- That model is not realistic or practical yet. It risks wasting tokens, doing the wrong work, missing acceptance criteria, and failing to complete work correctly.
- For now, sessions are still started manually for specific tracks, tickets, or ad hoc tasks.
- The existing structured handoff already separates planning from implementation and isolates implementation from question-and-answer cycles.
- The current orchestration model can run multiple workflow steps and subagents, but it is usually limited to isolated goals and often does not carry a track to full completion.
- The Iteration Agent already helps review and close implementations so the next increment can start.

## Missing capability

We still need a true merge and pickup system that can:

- merge sessions that began independently but converged on the same work,
- redistribute work from several overlapping sessions,
- represent many-to-many relationships between sessions and handoffs,
- keep a provenance chain showing which session handed work off to which other session and which session picked up whose work,
- associate multiple sessions with a track, and
- represent tracks that overlap, depend on one another, or contain smaller tracks.

## Example

If three sessions in the Session API project separately improve session transcript cost gating, handoff references, and track management, but their work starts to depend on each other, they should no longer be treated as three unrelated sessions. They should be merged into a shared session or shared track that can absorb the prior work and context, complete the overlapping part, and later hand the work back out again when the tracks diverge.

## Required workflow

The system must support a full cycle where:

1. We start from several separate requests.
2. One or more sessions work on them independently.
3. We merge those sessions into a shared track when they converge.
4. The shared track unlocks the dependent work.
5. Once the shared work is complete, the session can hand the tracks back out into separate specialized sessions.
6. Each merge or pickup preserves references to the originating sessions and their handoffs.

## Track structure

- A track is a larger connected system of related tickets rooted in an epic or tracker ticket.
- A track can contain a graph or tree of sessions linked by references.
- Sessions should work on the smallest possible track they belong to.
- Smaller tracks must also know which larger tracks use them.
- The orchestrator may start multiple tracks, merge their handoffs into a shared dependency track, and later split them again so specialized sessions can continue.

## Planning process

We should not invent work that already exists in the plan. The process should be:

1. First interview the user to clarify the exact shape of the system.
2. Turn that into a rough overarching plan with goals and acceptance criteria.
3. Design the necessary components structurally.
4. Search the existing planning and implementation work to find matching components.
5. Reuse and extend existing plans where possible.
6. Only define new items when they are not already covered.
7. Keep asking architectural questions when needed.
8. Write the goals, acceptance criteria, and chosen design into specs before implementation.
9. Use a ticket first if needed to drive the spec work.
10. Start implementation only after the spec and sequencing are finalized.
11. Orchestrate the work through several subagents and sessions until the full track is implemented and validated.

## Worked example: orchestrator merge and split

- An orchestrator starts multiple tracks and itself works a larger track that depends on those smaller tracks.
- The smaller tracks are worked by subagents, each with its own session, running in parallel or on different branches.
- While working, those smaller agents can spawn further sessions on the same track, or start a smaller shared track that both of them depend on and use, started through the same session.

- Once the shared track's session ends, the orchestrator generates two handoffs again from it — one for each original track — so those tracks can continue with their newly unlocked tasks.
- When both original tracks finish, the orchestrator merges them once more into a single shared handoff or pickup for itself, so it can conclude: both of its tracks are done, they both completed the shared track, they completed their own tasks, and it can now close its own track and hand off to the next session.

- documents the exact work steps for the agents and makes them accessible, and
- breaks the whole plan into clearly defined, goal-oriented work steps so the improvement can be integrated into the system as quickly as possible.
